body.p: Claims 11, 14, 19, 20, 24, 29, and 30 are currently amended. Claims 1-10 were previously canceled. Claims 11-30 are currently pending.
Claims 20 and 30 are amended to overcome the objections to the claims. Applicant respectfully requests withdrawal of the objections.
Claims 11, 13-23, and 25-31 are rejected as being unpatentable over Jain et al. (US 2016/0287128) in view of Chahine et al. (US 2017/0056644). Claims 11 and 29 have been amended.
1. Jain does not teach or suggest "a plurality of textile-based ECG electrodes," as recited
by claims 11 and 29, as amended.

As an initial matter, the Office Action asserts that paragraph [0062] of Jain describes a plurality of textile-based ECG electrodes. However, Jain describes "contactless ECG sensors" provided in a fabric. As laid forth below, Jain's "contactless ECG sensors" are not textile-based ECG electrodes.

For example, claim 11, as amended, recites that the "textile-based ECG electrodes comprises interlaced conductive fibers for conducting a plurality of ECG signals with respect to the upper body of the user while in contact with skin of the user." Jain, on the other hand, describes it's "contactless sensors as being "specifically designed to capture high quality ECG from a patient without requiring direct electrical contact with the patient's skin. This allows placement of the sensors 10 at some distance from the patient and/or to be separated from the patient's skin by a fabric such as clothing, bedding, etc...." Jain at [0080]. In this regard, Jain asserts that it's teaching of "contactless ECG electrodes" "circumvents issues associated with contact electrodes by being contactless ...." Jain at paragraph [0020]. As such, one skilled in the art would not modify the contactless ECG sensors of Jain to arrive at the claimed "textile-based ECG electrodes."

Furthermore, as recited in MPEP § 2143.02, a proposed obviousness modification requires a reasonable expectation of success. There is no teaching or description as to how one skilled in the art could reasonably expect to modify the contactless ECG sensors disclosed in Jain to arrive at an operable textile-based ECG electrode as in the claim 11. Accordingly, Applicant submits that such a modification of the contactless ECG sensor of Jain would not have been obvious to one skilled in the art, and that the obviousness rejection should be withdrawn.
At least for these reasons, claims 11 and 29, and claims dependent therefrom, are considered to be patentable over the cited art.
2. Jain does not teach or suggest "at least one textile-based ECG generator electrode for
transmitting a generated signal through the patient's upper body" as recited by claims

Claims 11 and 29 are amended to clarify that the plurality of textile-based ECG electrodes include "at least one textile-based ECG generator electrode for transmitting a generated signal through the patient's upper body."

The Office Action asserts that paragraphs [0088]-[0089] of Jain describe at least one textile- based ECG generator electrode. However, Jain describes a sensor pad 7 comprising contactless ECG sensors 10 and a right leg drive generator 14, among other things. The right leg drive generator 14 is not described or suggested as being an ECG electrode. Paragraphs [0088]-[0089], and Fig. 8 (reproduced below), describe and show that the right leg drive generator 14 is separate from the contactless ECG sensors 10. Accordingly, Applicant submits that Jain fails to teach or suggest "at least one textile-based ECG generator electrode for transmitting a generated signal."
FIG.8
At least for these reasons, claims 11 and 29, and claims dependent therefrom, are considered to be patentable over the cited art.
3. Jain does not teach or suggest a controller configured to "determine at least one of the
plurality of textile-based ECG electrodes (i) is at least partially out of contact with skin
of the user and/or (ii) causes the generated signal that is transmitted through the at
least one textile-based ECG generator electrode to be of unacceptable signal quality,"
as recited by claims 11 and 29.
Claims 11 and 29 are amended to clarify that the controller is configured to "based on the

collected signal, determine at least one of the plurality of textile-based ECG electrodes (i) is at least partially out of contact with skin of the user and /or (ii) causes the generated signal that is transmitted through the at least one textile-based ECG generator electrode to be of unacceptable signal quality.

As described in section 1 above, Jain is directed to contactless ECG sensors. Thus, Jain fails to teach a controller configured to determine that "at least one of the plurality of textile-based ECG electrodes is (i) at least partially out of contact with skin of the user."

Furthermore, as described in section 2 above, Jain does not transmit a generated signal through at least one textile-based ECG generator electrode. Thus, Jain fails to teach a controller configured to determine that "at least one of the plurality of textile-based ECG electrodes... (ii) causes the generated signal that is transmitted through the at least one textile-based ECG generator electrode to be of unacceptable signal quality."
In contrast, the present claims advantageously allow "the controller 14 to analyze the

collected signals 6b over time and thus decide if a change in sensors 18 being used in the sensor pairing for ECG signal 6a,b collection is needed, in view of determined signal quality. As such, it is recognised that over time, a deemed acceptable sensor 18 pairing (e.g. a selected actuator sensor 18 of the generation group 24 with a selected receiver sensor 18 of the receiver group 26) can be dynamically changed during the ongoing signal generation and collection." Present application at paragraph [0026].. At least for this reason, claims 11 and 29 are considered to be patentable over the cited art.
4. Jain fails to teach or suggest that "the controller detects whether one or more of the
plurality of textile-based ECG electrodes are in acceptable contact with the skin of the
user," as recited by claim 13.
The Office Action asserts that paragraph [0039] of Jain describes the controller detects

whether one or more of the plurality of textile-based ECG electrodes are in acceptable contact with the skin of the user. However, as described above, Jain describes contactless ECG sensors and not textile-based ECG electrodes comprising interlaced conductive fibers for conducting a plurality of ECG signals with respect to the upper body of the user while in contact with skin of the user. Thus, the controller is not configured to detect whether the plurality of textile-based ECG electrodes are in acceptable contact with the skin of the user.
At least for this reason, in addition to the dependency on allowable independent claim 11, claim 13 is considered to be patentable over the cited art.
5. One skilled in the art would not modify the controller of Jain to determine "a percentage
of contact surface area of one or more of the plurality of textile-based ECG electrodes
with the skin of the user," as recited by claim 12.

Similarly to point 4 above, Jain does not teach textile-based ECG electrodes comprising interlaced conductive fibers for conducting a plurality of ECG signals with respect to the upper body of the user while in contact with skin of the user, and therefore, does not have a controller configured to determine "a percentage of contact surface area of one or more of the plurality of textile-based ECG electrodes with the skin of the user." At least for this reason, in addition to the dependency on allowable independent claim 11, claim 12 is considered to be patentable over the cited art.
